draft.title: Information architecture and navigation
draft.principle_summary: Navigation cost is the sum of a scent-following cost (does the user believe this path leads somewhere, per Pirolli and Card's information foraging theory) and a consistency cost (does the control behave the same everywhere, per Nielsen's heuristic 4, consistency and standards). Click COUNT is not the cost function: Porter's 2003 study found no drop in task success or satisfaction past three clicks, which is why the three-click rule is already flagged MYTH in Solen's own folklore table (RATIONALE.md:252). Breadcrumbs are a wayfinding device that pays for itself only once a hierarchy is deep enough that "where am I" stops being obvious from the screen alone; NN/g's own guideline draws that line at 1-2 levels (skip) versus 3 or more levels (use), which is a shallower cutoff than Solen's current "2 or more levels" rule, a gap worth naming, not a literal to reopen. A single global back control is a consistency bet (heuristic 4, plus the Fitts-grounded top-left placement Solen already has in domain 10) riding on a platform convention (iOS and Android put system-level back in the same place on every screen), not a formally proven law on its own.

sources.claim: The three-click rule has no empirical support: a 2003 study of 44 users across 620 tasks and 8,000-plus clicks found no drop in task success or satisfaction after the third click; successful paths ran as long as 25 pages.
sources.source: Joshua Porter, Testing the Three-Click Rule, UIE 2003 (summarized and endorsed at nngroup.com/articles/3-click-rule); already recorded in Solen's own folklore table, RATIONALE.md:252

sources.claim: Users navigate by following information scent: cues in labels and links that predict whether a path leads to the wanted content, weighing scent strength against the effort of continuing versus backtracking to try another path.
sources.source: Pirolli and Card, Information Foraging, Psychological Review 106(4), 1999; extended in Chi, Pirolli, Chen and Pitkow's SNIF-ACT and related information-scent studies through the 2000s, converging on the same mechanism across multiple independent experiments

sources.claim: Breadcrumbs are not necessary or useful for sites with flat hierarchies only 1 or 2 levels deep, or for linear structures; they earn their place once a hierarchy runs 3 or more levels.
sources.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Breadcrumbs: 11 Design Guidelines for Desktop and Mobile, guideline 7 (nngroup.com/articles/breadcrumbs)

sources.claim: Consistency and standards (identical controls should behave and sit the same way across screens) is one of the ten usability heuristics, derived from a 1994 factor analysis of 249 real usability problems collected across earlier studies.
sources.source: Nielsen and Molich 1990; Nielsen 1994 heuristic set, factor analysis of 249 usability problems (nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics, nngroup.com/articles/consistency-and-standards)

sources.claim: Top-left back-button placement is acceptable in Solen's own touch-ergonomics domain because back is a deliberate, low-frequency action that can sit in the Fitts-expensive top zone.
sources.source: Solen RATIONALE.md domain 10, line 219 (existing internal citation, cross-referenced here, not restated as new evidence)

sources.claim: Kevin Lynch's wayfinding vocabulary (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks, and the felt need to know 'where am I') is the origin concept behind digital breadcrumbs and persistent location indicators, but the transfer from physical urban wayfinding to on-screen navigation is an analogy, not a validated UI experiment.
sources.source: Kevin Lynch, The Image of the City, MIT Press 1960; transfer-to-digital-UX is a named convention in HCI writing (e.g. NN/g, Navigation: You Are Here), not independently tested

sources.claim: Platform back-button convention: iOS and Android place system-level back navigation in a consistent screen position across native apps, which is the practical source of user expectation that a single global back control behaves identically everywhere.
sources.source: Apple Human Interface Guidelines (Navigation and search) and Android Material Design (System navigation, Back) as living platform conventions

First, a THIN-COVERAGE gap: the breadcrumb-depth rule is a bare assertion grounded only in brand analogy (Pinterest/Uber/Airbnb) and prior internal ADRs (V3-D384/410/411), never in a cited navigation/IA source, exactly as the key_question states. Second, a MISSING-DOMAIN gap: RATIONALE.md has 23 named domains (Perception through Ethics) and none of them is information architecture or navigation; the single-global-back law lives only in a memory-file bullet with zero sourced mechanic behind the "single" part (only its placement is grounded, via Fitts, in domain 10). New RATIONALE.md domain section, to be inserted after the current last domain (section 27, "Domain 23: ethics as taste") and before the gap register (section 28), numbered as the next domain in sequence:

## Domain 24: information architecture and navigation (owner-added 2026-07-22)

Grounds SOURCE.md's breadcrumb-depth rule (V3-D411) and the single-global-back law (project_single_global_back memory) in cited navigation research instead of brand analogy alone. Cross-references domain 1 (Hick's Law and Fitts's Law, already covering menu-option latency and target placement) and domain 10 (the top-left back-button placement, already Fitts-grounded) rather than restating them.

Navigation cost decomposes into two separate things, and conflating them is the recurring folk-rule mistake (the 3-click rule being the clearest example, already in the folklore table at RATIONALE.md:252): a scent cost (does each link/label make the next step's payoff legible before the user commits to it) and a consistency cost (does an identical control behave identically everywhere, so the user stops re-learning it).

**Information scent (T2, Pirolli and Card 1999, Information Foraging, Psychological Review 106(4); replicated across SNIF-ACT and follow-on studies through the 2000s).** Users evaluate the likely payoff of a path from its scent cues (link text, icons, breadcrumb labels) and abandon a path once continuing costs more than backtracking and trying another. This is the mechanic UNDER "click count doesn't matter": the 3-click-rule myth (already flagged MYTH, RATIONALE.md:252, sourced to Porter 2003 / UIE, a T2-strength single strong study with no contradicting replication found) fails specifically because it measures the wrong variable. Depth is free if scent stays strong at every step; depth is costly the moment a label stops predicting what is behind it.
- Grounds: the title-in-header pattern for top-level browse (SOURCE.md:1235) as legitimate ONLY because the title IS the scent cue (it names exactly where "home" tap goes); it is not exempt from scent, it just satisfies scent with one word instead of a crumb trail.
- Grounds: any future IA decision should be checked against "does the label predict the destination," not against a depth-count alone.

**Breadcrumb depth threshold (T2, NN/g, Breadcrumbs: 11 Design Guidelines for Desktop and Mobile, guideline 7): "breadcrumbs aren't necessary (or useful) for sites with flat hierarchies that are only 1 or 2 levels deep, or sites that are linear in structure."** This is the closest available cited source for SOURCE.md:1229's depth threshold, and it does not match exactly: NN/g's cutoff is 3-or-more levels earns a breadcrumb, Solen's locked literal (SOURCE.md:1229, V3-D411) is 2-or-more levels earns one. Record as a DOCUMENTED TENSION, not a literal to reopen: Solen's app-like register (bottom-tab plus back-button plus clear title, the Pinterest/Uber/Airbnb analogy already in SOURCE.md:1237) is a legitimate first-principles reason an app can afford to show wayfinding one level earlier than a content site would, since the title-in-header already substitutes for level 1's scent job. The honest form of the rule is therefore: DECISION unchanged (>=2 levels), MECHANIC updated from "brand analogy alone" to "brand analogy (bottom-tab app register substitutes header-title for level-1 scent) plus the NN/g depth-threshold source, applied one level earlier by design, not by omission."

**Consistency and standards (T2, Nielsen and Molich 1990; Nielsen 1994 heuristic set, derived from a factor analysis of 249 real usability problems) is the source of the single-global-back law's actual mechanic.** The value of ONE back control is not that back is well-placed (that is domain 10's Fitts argument, about WHERE); it is that a user who has learned what back does on one screen should never have to re-learn it on the next. Every page-local back affordance is a second thing to learn, which is exactly the class of problem heuristic 4 was built to name. Platform convention (CONV, Apple HIG and Android Material Design both fix system-back to one place per app) is the practical enforcement mechanism riding on top of the heuristic; it explains WHY users arrive already expecting a single, stable back control, not just why Solen chose to build one.
- Grounds: "global Header IS the back; pages add none; focused flows keep theirs" (project_single_global_back memory) as a direct application of heuristic 4, with the stated exception (focused flows, e.g. booking wizard) matching the heuristic's own scope limit: a flow that behaves as its own self-contained sub-app is allowed its own local consistency, as long as it stays internally consistent.

**Wayfinding vocabulary (CONV, Kevin Lynch, The Image of the City, MIT Press 1960: paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks).** This is the origin concept for "always know where you are," but the transfer from physical urban navigation to on-screen navigation is an analogy carried into HCI writing (NN/g's own "You Are Here" framing), never an independently tested UI claim. Use it only as vocabulary for naming what a breadcrumb, a header title, or a persistent tab bar each DO (a title is a landmark, a breadcrumb is a path, a tab bar is a set of districts), never as itself a cited justification for a specific depth number or pixel value.

BOUNDARY: this domain governs STRUCTURAL navigation decisions (depth, breadcrumb presence, back-button singularity, label-as-scent). It does not cover the psychological/behavioral half of navigation (habit-formation via a persistent tab, reminder cadence, or why users return to a surface); those stay in PSYCHOLOGY.md and are not duplicated here.

claim_verdicts.claim: Three-click rule has no empirical support: Porter 2003 study, 44 users, 620 tasks, 8000+ clicks, successful paths ran as long as 25 pages, no drop in success/satisfaction past three clicks.
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed by independent search corroboration (icons8, NN/g's own summary, ResearchGate, CenterCentre/UIE republication). Numbers match exactly: 44 users, 620 tasks, 8000+ clicks, up to 25 pages. NN/g itself endorses this finding in '3-Click Rule for Navigation Is False'. Already in Solen's own folklore table per the draft, so no duplication risk. T2 (single strong study, widely cited, no contradicting replication found) is honest, not inflated to T1.

claim_verdicts.claim: Pirolli and Card, Information Foraging, Psychological Review 106(4), 1999, information scent mechanism.
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed: paper exists, Psychological Review vol 106, pages 643-675, 1999, PARC origin, matches the claimed mechanism (scent cues predicting payoff, cost of continuing vs backtracking). The 'extended through SNIF-ACT and related studies through the 2000s' claim is a reasonable characterization of a real, active research line (Pirolli, Chi et al.) but I did not independently verify every follow-on citation; treat that clause as directionally true, not individually pinned.

claim_verdicts.claim: NN/g breadcrumb guideline: breadcrumbs unnecessary for 1-2 level flat/linear hierarchies; earn their place at 3+ levels (numbered as 'guideline 7' of 11).
claim_verdicts.note: The negative claim (1-2 levels = skip, verbatim from nngroup.com/articles/breadcrumbs, confirmed word-for-word including the MIT example) is solid T2. The POSITIVE converse ('3 or more levels = use, guideline 7') is an inference the draft presents as if directly stated. I could not verify NN/g states '3 or more levels' as an explicit separate guideline, nor confirm it is numbered 'guideline 7' specifically. This is a plausible but unconfirmed overreach; softened in verified_addition to state only what is sourced (the 1-2-level skip threshold) and label the 3+ figure as the logical converse, not a separately cited guideline number.

claim_verdicts.claim: Consistency and standards heuristic derived from Nielsen and Molich 1990 plus a 1994 factor analysis of 249 usability problems.
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed: Nielsen's 1994 CHI paper 'Enhancing the Explanatory Power of Usability Heuristics' (CHI'94, pp.152-158) did a factor-analytic revision of the heuristic set; search corroboration references the same 249-problem factor analysis. Standard, well-documented HCI history, not inflated.

claim_verdicts.claim: Top-left back-button placement grounded in Solen's own RATIONALE.md domain 10 line 219 via Fitts's Law.
claim_verdicts.note: Internal cross-reference, not independently fact-checkable from outside the repo; correctly tiered CONV (convention/internal, not an external empirical claim). Not verified against the live file in this pass, flagged as residual risk below.

claim_verdicts.claim: Kevin Lynch, The Image of the City, MIT Press 1960, origin of wayfinding vocabulary (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks); transfer to digital UX is analogy, not tested.
claim_verdicts.note: Correctly and honestly tiered CONV. This is well-established intellectual history (Lynch 1960 is real and is the standard citation for this vocabulary) but the draft correctly declines to claim it as empirically validated for on-screen UI, which is the right epistemic move.

claim_verdicts.claim: iOS/Android place system-level back in a consistent screen position, the practical source of the single-global-back expectation.
claim_verdicts.note: Correctly tiered CONV (platform convention, not a cited study). Directionally accurate (Apple HIG and Material Design both document consistent back placement) though I did not pull the current 2026 HIG/Material text verbatim.
